title: Tuneable terahertz transitions in zigzag graphene nanoribbons
authors: R. R. Hartmann, M. E. Portnoi
abstract: We show that a transverse electric field applied to a zigzag graphene nanoribbon opens a band gap whose energy can be tuned through the terahertz (THz) range. The field breaks the reflection symmetry of the ribbon, allowing optical transitions that are forbidden in its absence. The relative strengths of transitions polarized parallel and transverse to the ribbon depend strongly on excitation frequency and become equal at a particular frequency. At this frequency, each helicity selectively excites carriers in only one of the two field-induced edge-state valleys, with the selected valley reversed for the opposite helicity. Since this excitation occurs away from the valley minima, the photoexcited carriers have finite group velocity, giving rise to a circular photogalvanic response. Van Hove singularities enhance radiative recombination at the band edge, providing a route towards compact, tunable THz emitters.
summary: This theoretical study demonstrates that applying a transverse electric field to zigzag graphene nanoribbons opens a tunable band gap in the THz range. This field breaks symmetry, enabling polarization-selective optical transitions. The resulting phenomena, including a circular photogalvanic response, suggest zGNRs are promising platforms for compact, tunable THz emitters.
main_problem: The paper investigates how applying a transverse electric field to zigzag graphene nanoribbons (zGNRs) can open a tunable band gap in the terahertz (THz) range, enabling novel optical transitions.
main_result: The electric field breaks the ribbon's reflection symmetry, leading to a gap that scales linearly with the field strength. This allows for tunable THz emission and the generation of a circular photogalvanic response.
method: The analysis uses a nearest-neighbour $\pi$-orbital tight-binding model solved via the transfer-matrix method and perturbation theory to calculate optical transition matrix elements.
model_or_system: The system is a zigzag graphene nanoribbon (zGNR) modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian. The effect of the transverse electric field is introduced as a symmetry-breaking perturbation.
key_observables: Tunable band gap ($\epsilon_g$), polarization anisotropy ($s_1$), and helicity-resolved transition strengths.
important_parameters: Transverse electric field strength ($E$), excitation frequency ($\omega$), and ribbon width ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the nearest-neighbour $\pi$-orbital tight-binding model and uses approximations for large $N$ and specific limits for perturbation theory.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the opening of the gap ($\epsilon_g$ vs. $E$), the polarization anisotropy ($s_1$ vs. $k_y$), and the selective excitation of carriers using circularly polarized light.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the gap opening due to symmetry breaking, to analyzing polarization anisotropy, and finally demonstrating the helicity selectivity leading to a circular photogalvanic response for THz emission.
why_interesting: The strong dependence of optical selection rules on external fields and the resulting tunable THz emission mechanism make this highly relevant for quantum optics and open quantum systems research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) The atomic structure of a zigzag graphene nanoribbon, N atoms wide, is shown. Such a nanoribbon is commonly referred to as a (N/2)-ZGNR, where N/2 is the number of zigzag carbon chains across the ribbon’s width. The carbon atoms in the unit cell are numbered, and the primitive lattice vectors of graphene, a1 and a2, are indi- cated, together with the two inequivalent atoms belonging to the A and B sublattices that form the honeycomb lattice. (b) Schematic of the experimental geometry used to apply an in-plane electric field transverse to the nanoribbon axis.

FIG. 3. Edge-state gap εg as a function of the transverse electric-field strength. The numerical results are shown in gold. From top to bottom, the black curves correspond to the 20-ZGNR (long-dashed), 10-ZGNR (solid), and 2-ZGNR (short-dashed). The results for the 10- and 20-ZGNRs are obtained from the analytical dispersion in Eq. (2), while the exact analytical result for the 2-ZGNR is derived in End Mat- ter, Appendix B.

FIG. 2. (a) Energy spectrum of a 20-ZGNR in the absence (dashed black curve) and presence (solid black curve) of a transverse electric field of strength 106 V m−1. (b) Enlarged view of the positive-energy region, showing the spectra of 2- , 10-, and 20-ZGNRs under the same applied field, together with the zero-field spectrum of the 20-ZGNR for reference. For the 10- and 20-ZGNRs, the numerical results (solid and dash-dotted black curves) are compared with the analytical dispersion given by Eq. (2) (gold curves). The 2-ZGNR spec- trum is obtained from the exact analytical result derived in End Matter, Appendix B (dark-blue curve).

FIG. 4. Optical matrix elements for transitions across the edge-state gap in a 20-ZGNR as functions of the longitudinal wavevector ky. The red and blue curves show |⟨x⟩|/a and |⟨y⟩|/a, respectively, where |⟨x⟩| = |⟨ψf|ˆx|ψi⟩| and |⟨y⟩| = |⟨ψf|ˆvy|ψi⟩|/ω. These correspond to light polarized transverse and parallel to the ribbon axis, respectively, with ℏω = εf −εi. The open circles show the results obtained from the analytical expressions and are plotted over the range in which the states remain edge-localized. The grey dashed line shows the shifted energy spectrum, allowing one to identify the values of ky corresponding to the strongest transitions.

FIG. 5. Normalized Stokes parameter s1 for linearly polarized excitation as a function of the longitudinal wavevector ky. The leftmost blue, middle grey, and rightmost dashed black curves correspond to the 2-, 10-, and 20-ZGNRs, respectively. The limits s1 = 1 and s1 = −1 correspond to purely x- and y-polarized transitions, respectively. The transverse electric- field strength is 1 MV m−1.
